title: Language Model Circuits Are Sparse in the Neuron Basis
claim: Choice of representation and basis strongly affects how small a faithful, complete circuit can be; raw neurons rival sparse autoencoders.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, shared x-axis, legend at right
description: Two side-by-side line plots share a log-scale x-axis labelled Circuit size, running from 1 to 1e7. The left panel is titled Faithfulness and the right panel is titled Completeness. The y-axis runs from about -0.3 to 1.5. Eight curves appear in each panel. Color encodes the representation: red for MLP activations, blue for MLP outputs, green for the residual stream and purple for attention. Line style encodes the basis: solid for neurons and dashed for SAE features. In the left panel, the solid red MLP-neuron curve rises sharply near 100 components and peaks above 1.5. Most other curves climb later and settle near 1.0. In the right panel, the curves decay from 1 to 0 as circuit size grows. The dashed purple attention-SAE curve drops steeply and goes negative. The legend sits to the right, grouped under Representation and Basis.
caption: Faithfulness and completeness for different choices of representation in the model (residual stream, attention, MLP activations, or MLP outputs) and basis (neurons or SAE) when applying Integrated Gradients, averaged over the 4 SVA tasks with paired data.
abstract: The high-level concepts that a neural network uses to perform computation need not be aligned to individual neurons (Smolensky, 1986). Language model interpretability research has thus turned to techniques which decompose the neuron basis into more interpretable units of model computation, such as sparse autoencoders (SAEs). However, not all neuron-based representations are uninterpretable. For the first time, we empirically show that MLP neurons are as sparse a feature basis as SAEs. We use this finding to develop an end-to-end gradient-based attribution pipeline for circuit tracing on the MLP neuron basis, which surfaces causally effective neurons on a variety of tasks. On a standard subject-verb agreement benchmark (Marks et al., 2025), a circuit of $\approx 10^2$ MLP neurons is enough to control model behaviour. On the multi-hop city-state-capital task from (Lindsey et al., 2025), we find a circuit in which small sets of neurons encode specific latent reasoning steps (e.g. mapping a city to its state), and can be steered to change the model's output. This work thus advances automated interpretability of language models without imposing additional training costs.
